content: Bronchiectasis is a significant cause of respiratory illness in both developing and developed countries. Antibiotics are commonly used as a standard treatment for this condition. However, it remains unclear whether short courses of antibiotics, defined as four weeks or less, are effective in managing bronchiectasis. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of short courses of antibiotics (lasting four weeks or less) in treating both acute exacerbations and stable bronchiectasis in adults and children, compared to placebo or usual care. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted by the Cochrane Airways Group. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, OLDMEDLINE, CINAHL, AMED, and PsycINFO were searched up to February 2011. Additionally, respiratory journals and meeting abstracts were manually reviewed. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized controlled trials involving adults and children diagnosed with bronchiectasis, either clinically or through imaging. Patients with cystic fibrosis were excluded from the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies based on their titles, abstracts, and citations. Only one study met the inclusion criteria, which precluded the possibility of conducting a meta-analysis. The single eligible study demonstrated a modest benefit of four weeks of inhaled antibiotic therapy in adults with bronchiectasis who had pseudomonas detected in their sputum, compared to placebo. However, no studies were identified that evaluated the use of oral or intravenous antibiotics, and no studies were conducted in children. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy of short courses of antibiotics in managing bronchiectasis in adults and children. Until more robust evidence becomes available, it is recommended to adhere to existing treatment guidelines.
